segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And I, brothers and sisters, could not speak to you as spiritual people, but as people of flesh, as infants in Christ.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: I gave you milk to drink, not solid food, for you were not yet able to take it. Indeed, even now you are still not able,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: for you are still fleshly. For where there is jealousy and strife among you, are you not fleshly and living in a merely human way?

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For when one says,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “I belong to Paul,”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and another,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “I belong to Apollos,”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: are you not merely human?

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: What then is Apollos? And what is Paul? Servants through whom you came to believe, each as the Lord gave to him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: I planted, Apollos watered, but God was making it grow;

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: so neither the one who plants is anything, nor the one who waters, but God, who makes it grow.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The one who plants and the one who waters are one, and each will receive his own reward according to his own labor,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: for we are God’s coworkers; you are God’s field, God’s building.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: According to the grace of God given to me, like a wise master builder I laid a foundation, and someone else is building on it. But let each one take care how he builds on it;

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: for no one can lay any foundation other than the one that is laid, which is Jesus Christ.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now if anyone builds on the foundation with gold, silver, precious stones, wood, hay, straw,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: each one’s work will become plain, for the day will make it clear, because it is revealed by fire; and the fire itself will test what kind of work each one has done.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: If the work anyone has built on it remains, he will receive a reward;

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: if anyone’s work is burned up, he will suffer loss, though he himself will be saved, but only as through fire.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Do you not know that you are God’s sanctuary and that the Spirit of God dwells in you?

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: If anyone destroys God’s sanctuary, God will destroy that person; for God’s sanctuary is holy, and that is what you are.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Let no one deceive himself. If anyone among you thinks he is wise in this age, let him become a fool so that he may become wise,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: for the wisdom of this world is foolishness in God’s sight. For it is written:

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: “He catches the wise in their craftiness,”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and again:

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: “The Lord knows the reasonings of the wise, that they are futile.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So let no one boast in human beings. For all things are yours,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: whether Paul or Apollos or Cephas or the world or life or death or things present or things to come—all are yours,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and you are Christ’s, and Christ is God’s.

notes.note: The Greek plural is grammatically masculine but was the ordinary way to address a mixed group of men and women. Paul is writing to the whole assembly at Corinth, so “brothers and sisters” says in English what the first hearers understood. Many recent translations do the same; others keep “brothers” and explain it in a footnote.

Paul uses two related adjectives. The one here means “made of flesh,” and the one in verse 3 (rendered “fleshly”) means “characterized by flesh,” that is, by ordinary human nature apart from God’s Spirit. The traditional “carnal” now suggests sexual sin, which is not the point; the failing in view is rivalry and faction. Scholars differ on how sharply the two adjectives should be distinguished, and some manuscripts interchange them.

notes.phrase: living in a merely human way
notes.note: Literally “walking according to a human being.” “Walk” is a common biblical idiom for the way one conducts one’s life. “Merely” is supplied here and in verse 4, where the Greek is simply “are you not human beings?” The contrast with the “spiritual” people of verse 1 shows that Paul means human and nothing more.

notes.traditional: labourers together with God / God’s fellow workers
notes.note: The Greek can mean “those who work together with God” or “coworkers (with one another) who belong to God.” The rendering keeps the possessive form, which allows either sense and preserves the threefold “God’s … God’s … God’s” of the sentence. Many interpreters favor the second sense, because the context stresses that Paul and Apollos are servants and that God alone gives growth.

“Wise” applied to a craftsman was normal Greek for “skilled,” and the same phrase occurs in the Greek version of Isaiah 3:3. The word is kept as “wise” because Paul is playing on the theme of wisdom that runs through these chapters. The “master builder” was the person who directed a building project on site, a different role from the modern architect.

This is the day of the Lord, the expected day of God’s judgment, which Paul’s readers would have recognized without further explanation (compare 1:8). Fire is a standard prophetic image for that judgment. Here it is pictured as testing the materials of a building.

notes.traditional: it shall be revealed by fire
notes.note: The subject of “is revealed” is not stated. Most interpreters take it to be the day, which arrives in fire; it could also be each person’s work, which is exposed by fire. The English “it” leaves the question as open as the Greek does.

The picture is of a builder who escapes through the flames of his own burning building: he gets out alive, but with nothing. Most interpreters understand it as a vivid image of a narrow escape. The verse was later drawn into discussions of purification after death, but the passage concerns the testing of the work of those who build up the community.

Greek has two words that English Bibles usually both translate “temple.” One names the whole complex with its courts. The one used here names the building where the deity dwells, and “sanctuary” keeps Paul’s image on that place. Most versions have “temple,” and “you are God’s temple” is deeply established in English. “You” is plural throughout: the community together is the one sanctuary.

notes.phrase: “He catches the wise in their craftiness,”
notes.note: The first quotation is Job 5:13, in wording that differs from the Septuagint as it has come down and stands closer to the Hebrew. The second, in verse 20, is Psalm 94:11 (93:11 in the Greek numbering). There the Psalm speaks of the thoughts “of people,” and Paul writes “of the wise” to fit his argument.

Cephas is the Aramaic name, meaning “rock,” of the apostle better known by its Greek equivalent, Peter. Paul normally uses the Aramaic form. Cephas was one of the figures around whom factions in Corinth had formed (1:12).

candidates.reason: The plural address to mixed congregations occurs throughout the letters and Acts, and translators divide between “brothers,” “brothers and sisters” and “friends,” so one policy is needed.
With σάρκινος and the wider σάρξ vocabulary it recurs across Paul, and “carnal,” “worldly,” “of the flesh” and “fleshly” all compete; it should be fixed alongside the decision for σάρξ.
The figurative “walk” for conduct is frequent in Paul and John, and a decision is needed on whether to keep the Semitic idiom “walk” or render it “live” uniformly.
A key Pauline word that versions render “boast,” “glory,” “take pride” or “exult”; varying it obscures a theme that links Romans, 1–2 Corinthians, Galatians and Philippians.
It ranges over “test,” “prove,” “examine,” “approve” and “discern” across the letters, and readers lose the thread when the English shifts without a governing decision by sense.
